Hi all. I'm new to this community. I'd been hearing about it over on reddit and finally decided to check it out. My impetus was more academic than social: I was interested in doing some text mining and analysis on various subreddits (of a fairly large scale) and the reddit API wasn't particularly good at supporting giant leeches like I intended to be. So while I was poking around, I figured I'd take a look over here to see if maybe things are a little more bite-sized.

I actually really like your v1 API. I mean, yes, it's not fully featured and doesn't quite have what I would need to do a full crawl, but it's cozy. I just spent a day writing a bunch of boiler-plate Java wrappers for it and it just works (except for the SSL cert, which required some jiggery-pokery on my end).

I've gathered that you're working on a new API, and I have the following requests:

  1. Please version your API. Please, please, please just do it. Make the requests look like ".../api/v2.0/foobar?foo=bar" or whatever you deem appropriate. I've been working with data vendor APIs for years in a professional capacity and while I'm sure you folks are on point, I wanted to get that out there.
  2. You have inconsistencies in your date formatting. Sometimes you use milliseconds, sometimes you don't, and this breaks any date parser that doesn't have a heuristic to catch that, which is most of them. IIRC, C#'s date facilities have a bunch of different formats that they'll try when parsing up a date string. Java's, on the other hand, do not. Please pick a format and stick with it for your v2 API, and consider shipping a new version of your v1 API (v1.1 or whatever, for backward compat) that fixes specifically this issue. I'd recommend keeping the milliseconds (which would look like "yyyy-MM-dd'T'hh:mm:ss.SSS" in the vernacular of date formatters).
  3. Your data types are a little funky. For instance, if I'm looking at a listing of subverses, it comes in the form of an array of simple strings in the JSON payload. That's fine, but I can also request a more replete composite type (which I've called SubverseInfo in my own wrappers). Similarly for badges, the user info request will yield an array of doubles of the form { badge name, awarded date }, whereas requesting the badge info by name yields a different structure. I guess my concern here is kind of trivial, but it does kind of result in some type bloat. Maybe that's okay, though. It just came off as a little idiosyncratic on first blush.

I'm not kitted out for C# development anymore, or I'd start chugging through your codebase. I did, however, read your announcement about the new API (which, again, I'm hoping is versioned and does not simply supplant your existing API out of the blue) and I'd be down to check it out. I can't guarantee a lot of throughput on my end, since my day job occupies a lot of time and energy and I tend to be very phasic with my interests. Still, it'd be interesting to see what changes you've introduced while I've got the v1 API so fresh on my mind.

FWIW, the little project on which I'm working is over here: voat-search on github. Check the dev branch for the time being - I haven't merged anything over to the master. I thought it might be nice to set up a Lucene index and stash crawl results into it for later analysis, maybe surface that feature to end-users. I'm very familiar with the vagaries of operating large-scale crawling, indexing operations and search engines, so please note that I do not currently have any intention to attempt to operate a full-scale, near-realtime, distributed, partitioned index, with all kinds of totally k-rad custom lexing and all that jazz. I wouldn't mind building it, but I can't afford to actually operate it, and I'm guessing you can't either. But if there's interest and you guys end up having the resources to operate a search engine with all kinds of cool features, that could be fun.

I'm wondering if maybe I should carve out the API wrapper from my little project, though, and make it a separate project. A lot of content-driven sites with APIs benefit from having readily accessible API wrapper support in a bunch of languages. I may be one of the three lonely assholes on the planet who is willing to do it in Java. I'd just need to figure out how to get things distributed (I'm relatively new to Maven and still haven't quite figured out how to get build and release environments and distribution channels provisioned for hobby projects). If anybody has knowledge of how opensource projects handle distribution, I'm all ears.

Anyway, nice work so far. I hope it continues to be rewarding for everyone involved.
